rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to stop at four real stories and keep each one closer to what can actually be proved. A is strong, but 'Duolingo Lets Subscribers Talk to an AI. The Question Is Whether It Can Replace a Human Tutor.' reaches past the supplied facts, and 'Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence' smuggles in causality. B's 'Duolingo adds chess, testing whether its habit machine works beyond language' is cleaner: sharp thesis, clear beat, honest proof gap.
gaps_in_A: 'The Question Is Whether It Can Replace a Human Tutor' overstates the competitive frame; the update supports conversation practice, not replacement of tutors.
'Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence' asserts a causal relationship the facts do not establish.
The platform angle and 'Why Duolingo Made Chess Free and AI Tutoring Expensive' overlap around the same expansion/monetization thesis; useful, but not fully clean separation.
Next step says '`meanest-editor`' before building a journalist list. For angle selection, the sharper next move is fit-checking reporters after proof gaps are answered.
gaps_in_B: 'AI cartoon' and 'talking cartoon' are punchy but not strictly supplied; the facts say character Lily, not cartoon.
'live spoken conversation practice is exactly what critics say apps lack' invents the critics' specific objection. The update only says some educators call gamification shallow.
The first angle leans on 'AI companions moving from chatbots into paid products' without an external peg supplied; it survives, but only because the product launch is real.
It leaves out A's useful human-tutor market counterposition, which could be pitchable if Duolingo has tutor-comparison data or credible outside reaction.
